#10567. Researchers are making Lego-like lunar dust bricks for building on the moon

There are plenty of techno-fantasies about living on the moon, but what would these lunar cities actually be made from? Blasting concrete, rebar, and big, bulky construction equipment into space isn’t feasible, so some scientists are exploring how to build a base on the moon using what’s already up there: moon dust.

Research from the University of Arkansas found that regolith, the loose lunar dust that covers the moon, could be used to 3D print Lego-like bricks that could one day be used in the construction of permanent structures. Their research, written up by Wan Shou, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering; Cole McCallum, then an undergraduate; and others, was published in NPJ Advance Manufacturing in August.

What makes 3D printing with locally available materials on the moon more difficult than on Earth is that the moon materials are harder to pack. This is because meteorites repeatedly crashing into Earth’s only natural satellite make its surface rough and jagged. There’s no wind or water to smooth things down, and nothing to bind the material together.

“Lunar dust is essentially finely broken rock,” Shou tells Fast Company. “Unlike typical soil on Earth, it contains no organic matter from plants or other organisms.”

Those irregular particles create a manufacturing challenge. They don’t spread and pack as evenly as the spherical powders commonly used in metal 3D printing, which makes it harder to produce uniform layers and consistent bonding.

Instead of actual moon dust, researchers used commercially available lunar regolith simulant, a synthetic material that approximates the way real lunar dust looks and behaves. To form the bricks, they used a form of 3D printing called laser powder bed fusion in which a high-powered light or laser fuses a fine layer of powder through a process called sintering. The team tested different laser conditions, then built thicker, multilayer specimens before forming several small interlocking bricks.

Other attempts to create building materials that would work with lunar dust have required additional binders, solvents, or processing materials. But the University of Arkansas researchers wanted to create with a method that was direct and binder-free so as to minimize the materials that would need to be transported from Earth.

To build on the prototype, Shou says they need to improve the bonding between layers, reduce defects, improve the mechanical performance, and refine the surfaces so the bricks can fit together more securely. From there, the next steps would be testing fabrication in a vacuum and with low gravity, as well as testing durability through repeated temperature changes.

“Making an interlocking brick is an encouraging first step,” Shou says. “A construction system will require predictable performance across both individual bricks and assembled structures.”

Shou says they envision that in the future, there’s a possibility of using concentrated light directly to do a similar fabrication. If it works, that’s a simple recipe for a basic structure made from just two ingredients: a moon base made from moon dust and sunshine.

#10566. Google Play wants Android apps to nail foldable basics by April 2027

Google Play is introducing new adaptive app and game quality requirements next year to elevate the Android foldable experience.

Starting April 2027, the Play Store will require developers to meet Tier 3 of the Android adaptive app quality guidelines for foldables.

Referred to as “Adaptive ready” or “basic” support, Tier 3 requires apps not to use letterboxing (or other compatibility modes) and to fill the entire screen. During rotation, resizing, and folding/unfolding, apps must preserve scroll position, text input, and media playback. Apps must also support multi-window environments.

Apps that do not meet this quality bar will no longer be able to publish or update on Google Play, and may have reduced visibility on the store.

At the same time, Google Play will require foldable device screenshots for app listings: “Providing foldable screenshots by April 2027 will become a standard submission requirement when publishing new apps or updating your store listing.”

Curious to see whether the requirements will actually be as strict as they make them seem (on paper).

If so, then also Google will have a ton of work to do to modernise all of their apps.

By August 2027, new and updated apps will be required to target Android 17 (API level 37).

Over time, this “quality framework will progressively expand to incorporate Tier 2 and Tier 1 standards across foldables, tablets, Googlebooks, and Android XR.”

Apps that meet Tier 2 (better) or Tier 1 (best) will get “premier store badging, editorial spotlighting, and enhanced merchandising across Google Play as the platform bar elevates.”

On the gaming front, titles will need to add foldable screenshots to listings by April 2027, while Tier 3 large screen quality guidelines go into effect in August 2027.

#10563. J.Crew’s new Miles Davis capsule honors the jazz icon’s preppy style

Miles Davis was arguably as famous for his fashion as he was for his music—American Ivy suits, African dashikis, and textured Issey Miyake shirts were all part of his wardrobe.

Now, 100 years after the artist’s birth, J.Crew has released a limited-edition capsule collection inspired by his legendary style and the American heritage look that is at J.Crew’s core. Launched November 20, the collection includes a T-shirt, an Oxford shirt, and a baseball cap.

“From his tailored suits and Ivy League-inspired wardrobe to the way he mixed classic pieces with a more individual, unconventional sensibility, Miles helped shape a look that continues to influence today,” says Golnar Khosrowshahi, founder and CEO of music rights company Reservoir Media. (Reservoir acquired 90% of Davis’s music publishing catalog last year, alongside shared control of his name, image, and likeness).

The lasting style is apparent in the capsule’s three objects. First, there’s a co-branded Oxford shirt, technically a J.Crew 1983, that is an homage to the mint-green button-down Davis wore on the cover of his 1958 album Milestones. To help the shirt hang just like the one on the album, J.Crew opted for a “heritage fit” that features a slightly longer collar and substantial weight from the 100% woven cotton, resulting in a relaxed take on the classic.

Then there’s a vintage-wash cotton shirt emblazoned with an illustration of Davis. The reference image dates back to 1970, photographed by Glen Craig at a performance at the Fillmore East in New York City.

Lastly, a classic black baseball cap is adorned with Davis’s signature, embroidered in vibrant blue thread against the rugged-wash canvas.

The collection follows a series of limited-edition drops from J.Crew, which has partnered with the New York Fire Department and The New Yorker as part of the retailer’s broader post-bankruptcy strategy to be at the “center of culture.”

“Collaborations create a meaningful entry point for people who may know Miles Davis well and are discovering J.Crew through the collection, while giving longtime J.Crew customers a new perspective on familiar pieces,” a J.Crew spokesperson tells Fast Company. “They help us keep our classics in the cultural conversation.”

It’s not surprising that the clothing company would want to feature the most well-known jazz musician of the 20th century in its product line. But for Khosrowshahi, landing on J.Crew as a partner for Davis’s centennial celebration was a way of highlighting Davis’s legacy beyond music, focusing on fashion instead.

“The goal isn’t to put an artist’s name on as many products as possible; it’s to find the right collaborators and create experiences that reflect the artist’s identity, values, and influence,” Khosrowshahi says. “This J.Crew collaboration is one example of how we’re bringing that broader vision to life.”

The collection also brings Davis into the smaller details. The inside labels pair the J.Crew logo with a red silhouette of Davis playing the trumpet in place of the classic J.Crew Oarsman. The items’ tags also stand out for featuring Davis’s signature.

The capsule is available online and at select J.Crew stores, including Bond Street, Rockefeller Center, and Fifth Avenue in New York City; Century City in Los Angeles; Newbury Street in Boston; North Michigan Avenue in Chicago; and Georgetown in Washington, D.C.

“Preserving Miles’ legacy doesn’t mean keeping it frozen in time,” a spokesperson from the Miles Davis Estate says. “Miles was always looking ahead, always experimenting, and always pushing boundaries. Whether through music, fashion, visual art, or other creative collaborations, we want people to recognize just how far his influence extends.”

#10561. How do brands measure customer experiences when AI does the shopping?

Let’s take a step back to the dotcom era. When companies moved from brick and mortar to e-commerce, businesses scrambled to figure out CX strategies that would attract and retain customers online. Search engine optimization, cookies, and tech innovations quickly followed to infer as much as possible about consumer intent, journeys, and experiences. Today, brands are still trying to understand these signals, but there’s a new twist. 

As purchasing power shifts to artificial intelligence agents like Meta Muse, OpenAI Dots, and Instinct AI, consumers won’t navigate web pages and mobile applications; they’ll tell their digital proxies what they want and let the agent do the work. This change will upend traditional notions of marketing, personalization, e-commerce, and customer experience.

After a consumer agent interacts with a company, how will the company understand the experience? Why did the agent pick Store A versus Store B? Will the agent explain their decision process? How will the agent traverse digital assets? How much information will an agent share with companies during interactions? And how can a brand measure the customer’s “customer experience” when the buyer isn’t directly interacting with the brand?

What Agents Mean for Consumers

Customer experiences have endured seismic change over the past few decades. In the late 1990s, the dotcom era introduced digital disintermediation, and leaders like Amazon and Walmart leaped ahead of traditional department stores, specialty retailers, and shopping malls that failed to adapt their business models. Years later, as smartphones became pervasive, consumers moved to the new medium. Successful organizations adopted unified customer profiles across devices, geolocation and tracking technologies, and even more surgically precise personalization to create more relevant, quality experiences.

Agentic commerce will drive another CX revolution across marketing, sales, and service. But to understand how companies should respond, we need to start with what this shift means for consumers. 

A personalized AI agent can do more. While an agent is powered by the same underlying technology that drives large language models like Gemini and Claude, it does more than answer questions or make recommendations. When you ask an agent to do something, it interviews you to understand your preferences and remembers past experiences. It takes the initiative to scour the internet, make calls, comparison shop, make reservations, order deliveries, and call or chat with customer support on your behalf to make sure you get what you want. You tell it what you want, and it does the work.   

As consumers embrace personal agents, this convenience means people will spend less time and effort shopping, buying, and interacting with brands. The traditional omni-channel, customer-led journey—reading reviews, shopping online, and dealing with a mix of chatbots, voice bots, and frontline employees— will be driven less by the consumer and more by the agent. Understanding and establishing customer satisfaction, loyalty, and brand equity will require new tools and techniques.

What Agents Mean for Brands

We’re just beginning this transition to an agentic experience. When agents mediate product discovery and purchasing decisions on a customer’s behalf, data and signals showing whether the interaction drove the desired outcomes are obscured. That requires a better understanding of what happens during agentic interactions themselves. 

The CX business was built on surveys and scores like the Net Promoter Score (NPS). But NPS has always been a proxy for how likely a customer is to do business with a brand again. Real loyalty measures are behavioral, like how recently they engaged with the brand, the quality of the interaction, or how consistently they spent with the company. 

Traditional measures like those work when customers can directly reflect on an interaction, but they don’t tell the whole story when AI agents handle it. Brands still need to distinguish between completing a transaction and meeting the customer’s needs. Without connecting signals, businesses can lose sight of the overall relationship.

What Brands Can Do About It

As with any disruptive technology, we will see some businesses adapt to this new era of personalized agents more successfully than others. Companies will face the challenge of learning how to optimize their business model to work with agents without compromising the quality and efficiency of an evolving customer experience.

Agents may not need to share customer preferences or details with companies to be effective, but organizations should create incentives for them to do so. Today, a customer who provides a rewards number can earn rewards. With the right incentives, customer agents should still do so.

Brands should build corporate agents that can communicate richly and honestly with customer agents. Agents, like humans, thrive on information. The more information a corporate agent exchanges with a customer agent, the better the agents can make informed, relevant decisions.

The key is to listen everywhere. Don’t treat this new channel as if it doesn’t have context. Connect customer agentic interactions with digital, conversational, and in-person interactions into journeys and outcomes. By doing so, organizations can uncover critical insights, interests, and motivations that would otherwise remain hidden within the agentic black box.

The New CX

New technology often creates uncertainty. Think of when music moved from physical discs to digital platforms like iTunes or Spotify. Some record labels resisted giving up the physical relationship they built with fans, but eventually, to be relevant, labels embraced the new media.

Brands may see agentic commerce as a similar threat to customer experience control. But brands that leverage these new channels to build relationships with new and existing customers will find that AI agents present a tremendous opportunity for insight rather than an existential threat.

A small but welcome potential reprieve for PC builders and consumers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Solid-state drives, phones, laptops, and tablets have all gotten substantially pricier in the last couple of years. Beyond the stratospheric prices of DDR5 memory, prospective PC builders and consumer electronics buyers have had to deal with upcharges on SSDs of all sizes thanks to the AI boom. That may be changing soon, as spot pricing for consumer NAND chips is reportedly dropping, according to a new report from Seoul Economic Daily (SED).

The report observes a 20% drop in spot pricing for NAND chips over just the last month. Its conclusions are bolstered by information from a Bank of America note from Nov. 13, wherein industry sources tell that institution that NAND is due for a market correction.

SED says that according to that note, 512 Gb NAND wafers saw a 32% drop to $14.30 apiece on the spot market, while 1 Tb wafers fell 19% to $24.90. SED quotes another industry source that says: "NAND cannot sustain the steep price gains seen so far."

Those decreases may be hard to square in a time when enterprise SSDs are getting pricier by the day, but SED notes that the rise in phone and PC prices has led customers to delay upgrades, resulting in a 20% year-on-year decline in shipments for phones alone and making for the lowest third-quarter volumes in 14 years. Meanwhile, PC shipments have also fallen 22.5% year-on-year, according to a Gartner report.

In the face of those consumer decisions, device makers are letting their existing stock drain out and are presumably stocked with NAND chips for the short term, thus resulting in lower prices for new fab shipments on the short-term spot market.

Another factor in the consumer NAND market is that not all flash is equal. Both RAM and NAND makers have been redirecting their chip output to serve the ongoing AI boom, converting their consumer-grade production lines to make higher-spec silicon. Memory factories have been converting DDR5 capacity to HBM at a steady pace, as parts of the process are shared across both types.

But according to the Bank of America note that SED cites, things are different in the NAND world. High-density flash now sits at around 300 layers, and its production requires substantially different tooling compared to the lower-grade silicon deemed suitable for us mere mortals. So the continuing growth in NAND demand from AI data centers may not translate directly into reduced consumer supply.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Beyond those factors, added supply from Chinese NAND maker YMTC is creating additional downward price pressure in the NAND market. SED notes that YMTC has taken a 14% chunk from major players in the NAND market in the second quarter of this year alone.

On net, these forces could result in a bit of relief for consumer tech. SED says Bank of America expects consumer NAND prices for PCs and smartphones to fall 5% to 10% on the longer-term contract market in the first quarter of 2027, while enterprise NAND contract prices are expected to hold more or less steady.

Whether those declines translate to lower prices for finished devices and components like SSDs will remain to be seen, and products with those chips inside will require some time to reach the market. But in the ongoing AI supply crunch, any potential relief is worth celebrating.

#10558. How Anthropic believes branding will shape its post-IPO future

Anthropic enjoyed a singularly blockbuster debut on the Nasdaq yesterday, shrugging off any concerns about going public at a moment when the artificial intelligence industry faces a strained public image. ANT priced at $83 a share, above expectations, making it the biggest IPO of all time, worth a staggering $1.5 trillion; it finished its first trading day at $97.17.

Investors are fundamentally betting on the technology underpinning Anthropic’s products and business. But in this case, it’s easy to overlook the importance of another factor that’s played a major role in the company’s remarkable rise: strong brand optics. Anthropic itself makes that case in its S-1 form, which gave investors a glimpse into the company’s thinking before its IPO. Tellingly, the word “brand” appears 63 times.

Admittedly, the S-1 is a book-length document covering many topics. But the filing reveals a company that recognizes how much branding has mattered in a razor-competitive category like AI—and how much it will matter in the future. 

Many of Anthropic’s rivals have launched on the backs of widely known brands or brand ecosystems: Google’s Gemini, Meta’s Muse, Elon Musk’s Grok, Microsoft’s Copilot. OpenAI became a household name thanks to the surprise popularity of its ChatGPT product, and an avalanche of publicity. Anthropic, by contrast, didn’t even exist until a few years ago, when a group broke away from OpenAI to found what was then an upstart rival. With a story specifically touting ethical responsibility and social trust, it leaned on a brand-forward identity from the start.

With notable exceptions—Apple especially—tech companies often treat branding as a squishy afterthought. Innovation and word of mouth, the thinking goes, drive success, not a promoted public image. Anthropic, no doubt, attributes its rapidly growing profile to its flagship chatbot, Claude, and other products establishing it as a world-class AI lab with enormous upside potential (and similarly extreme risks). 

But it’s worth unpacking what that filing had to say on the subject of growth. It argues that even a category-leading product depends on brand reputation, and offers insight into how Anthropic will pursue its branding goals after the IPO. Building on its founding proposition as the AI company with a conscience, Anthropic seeks to cement an image that commingles efficiency and trust, leveraging individual connection with its products to fuel enterprise growth.

For starters, Anthropic reports that its annual ad spending spiked from $33 million in 2024 to $147 million last year, and is expected to keep growing in 2026. (Notably, Anthropic advertised during the Super Bowl this year, poking at OpenAI for incorporating ads into its chat results.)

That may not sound like much for a company that reported $33 billion in revenue through the first nine months of 2026, but it’s clear that its brand strategy isn’t just a gloss, and in fact will help drive growth. 

“The promotion of our brand requires us to make substantial expenditures, which we anticipate will increase as our market becomes more competitive,” the filing explains. “If we do not successfully maintain and enhance our brand, our business may not grow, we may have reduced pricing power relative to competitors, we could lose customers.”

More specifically, Anthropic positions brand building as a way to become a recognizable, deliberately chosen collaborator to what it dubs “prosumers.” These individuals pay for AI tools to perform knowledge work and their personal product preferences can influence organizational purchasing like, say, bringing Claude into their workplaces. 

The filing doesn’t quite suggest that Anthropic thinks models are becoming commodities, or that branding will ultimately matter more than performance. But in effect, it argues that in an increasingly competitive market, the brand is going to matter a lot to consumers (or prosumers) who see rival products as somewhat interchangeable, and find it easy to jump from one to another.

And maybe more to the point: Many others see AI as a problem, spawning controversial data centers and threatening jobs. As the S-1 cautions, Anthropic’s brand must also contend with “broader public perceptions of the AI industry, and we may be grouped with other industry participants and judged similarly, regardless of differences in our approach or conduct.” 

The period just before Anthropic’s IPO was a rough stretch for the industry overall. It featured the Jensen Huang scandal at AI mainstay Nvidia, multiple air traffic and Internet failures that sparked (seemingly evidence-less) conspiracy theories centered on AI, and a handy New York Post quiz about surviving an “AI apocalypse.”

Thus Anthropic has been at pains to distinguish itself as the cautious and thoughtful AI company, clashing with the Pentagon about military uses of its technology, claiming to want more regulation, keeping advertising out of its products—and going public as a public benefit corporation, a structure meant to prod leadership to think beyond profits.

Not everyone is convinced. Critics accuse Anthropic leadership of having a “savior complex.” But it does seem remarkable that its IPO was such a roaring success despite a terrible stretch for the sector overall. The stock market measures investor sentiment, which is not quite the same as brand reputation—but also not totally unrelated. Anthropic’s brand may have aided its IPO’s success. And that success is certainly good for the brand.

NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today. A countdown at Orbital Radar confirmed that Voyager cruised past the threshold at a leisurely 37,844 mph just after 5 am ET on Wednesday, November 18. It means that Voyager is now more than 16 billion miles away, and that a signal from the spacecraft now takes fully 24 hours to travel the distance.

There are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat. Sci-fi shows casually mention light-years as if they are like a trip to the local convenience store. One light-day isn’t a distance to be derided, though. Over the last half century, hurtling through space at a cruising speed of 38,000 mph, the Voyager spacecraft has clocked about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers).

These are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming. So NASA has kindly provided some context with the distances of various heavenly bodies in miles and light-speeds. For example, the Moon is 238,855 miles distant, or about 1.3 light seconds away from Earth. Due to Mars’ independent orbit around the Sun, it can take between three minutes and 22 minutes for light to travel between the red and the blue planet. Meanwhile, the Sun’s rays reach Earth, about 93 million miles away, in 20 light seconds. Now let us remind you that Voyager 1 is on the brink of being a whole light-day away.

On Wednesday, with this major milestone passed, Voyager 1’s journey will be far from over. NASA says that it is on course for an obscure star called Gliese 445, now in the constellation Ursa Minor. We’ll have to keep the champagne on ice for another 40,000 years to celebrate the fly-past of that star, though.

Voyager 1 carries a copy of the Golden Record. Like sending a message in a bottle, NASA scientists launched Voyager with the hope that someone, somewhere will eventually read the message. Moreover, the receiving aliens will need to source tech to play the record, which contains sounds, music, and the data needed to reconstruct photos that showcase the diversity of life and culture on our planet.

If an alien got hold of the record on Wednesday and managed to rustle up a gramophone player to listen to it, a message sent to Earth via radio waves would take a full 24 hours to be received.

Space enthusiasts are also invited to participate in a global event “by creating a wave of golden light.” It sounds rather pointless, but enthusiasts are asked to flash the three-letter call sign for NASA's Voyager mission, VGR, into the night sky - Morse Code style - using their phone flashlights. There’s a website you can open to flash your screen appropriately.

#10555. 5 major network outages in three days: It’s not a conspiracy; it’s change

Like millions of other Americans, I was stuck at an airport on the infamous Friday the 13th in November when air traffic in the U.S. came to a halt. From where I sat at Fort Lauderdale airport, the panic was obvious. Crowds overflowed at gates. Hotel rooms disappeared quickly. I got one of the last ones available in the city. It was chaos.

That’s what happens when big networks go down: chaos. And it’s only just beginning unless organizations fix how they change their network infrastructures. 

Of course, the ground stop would have made news by itself. But what really got people talking was that it was one of a series of major outages that occurred over just a few days’ time. Shortly before the ground stop, a Microsoft Outlook outage left businesses unable to send email. Our company had contracts held up by it. And on Monday, November 16, customers at several major banks found they couldn’t reach their accounts.

Email, air travel, banking—three essential elements of the American economy, not to mention people’s daily lives—crashed in the span of just three business days. Suddenly, people who don’t know a router from a switch were talking about network infrastructure. Conspiracy theories multiplied on social media and in the dark corners of the internet. 

I spend my working life close to the networks behind failures like these, and I can say with complete confidence that there is no conspiracy here. The root cause of all the outages might sound less satisfying than a complex conspiracy theory, but it is daunting nonetheless: The infrastructure that runs the world is changing faster than ever, and change always brings risk. When organizations fail to manage changes in their network infrastructure, the result, as we all saw last week, can be chaos.

It almost always starts with a change

The issue at the root of network outages is almost always change. Based on what we know at this point, change was at the root of the air traffic control failure. The network that carries communications between the major air traffic control centers is decades old and in the middle of a long modernization, which involves moving from legacy protocols and transmission to modern fiber and new equipment.

At one step of that transition, when new network devices were introduced, something went wrong. A misconfiguration or a misbehaving device sent traffic into the network that other devices couldn’t handle. Those devices began to fail, and the failure cascaded. Shortly after, the rush to find a hotel room began.

The Outlook outage had the same origin: configuration changes, unintended consequences, knock-on failures. Some of the triggering configurations were already months old and sat quietly until a condition in the network finally exposed them.

Why can’t networks just heal themselves?

So, why do these outages occur? Networks are supposed to route around damage. In theory, they should. But in practice, change can shake up a network infrastructure in unpredictable ways. 

A network is, by definition, a set of interacting systems. Change one element and you change how its neighbors behave, and how their neighbors behave after that. Change is necessary. Unfortunately, it’s not always good, and when it’s bad it just gets worse as it travels through the network infrastructure.

That’s why the teams who run critical networks practice serious discipline before a change: pre-change testing, a mapped-out plan for every step, a rollback plan. I’m confident the people involved last week did all of that. But the interconnections inside a large network are so vast that no team can test for every eventuality. That’s not carelessness. It’s the nature of complex, interconnected systems. It could happen to even the most prepared team.

Redundancy helps, and these networks have layers of it. But redundancy does not remove complexity. In some ways, it adds to it.

Why recovery takes so long

So if a change caused the problem, the simple solution is to undo the change. But that’s not easy to do because the same interconnectedness that caused the failure makes it hard to reverse. A problem becomes exponentially more difficult to fix as it cascades through the network infrastructure and tangles itself into a complex web of systems. Here’s what has to happen for a team to fix an issue related to change:

  1. The team has to diagnose it. When effects cascade across the network, often it’s not obvious which change caused which symptom. This is where visibility becomes critical. You can’t fix what you can’t see. An accurate picture of the network, what’s connected to what, how each element should be configured, and what is happening right now can make the difference between a fast fix and one that takes many times longer while the team works in the dark.
  2. The team has to remediate, and rollback is just the start. By the time the team finds a cause, the problem has usually triggered other failures. Elements of the network infrastructure have to talk to one another again before the network works as it should. That process often has to happen in a careful order so the applications on top return cleanly. Microsoft’s team reportedly spent days painstakingly rebuilding its environment to avoid further knock-on effects.
  3. The team has to regain confidence that the problem won’t come straight back. The initial fix doesn’t always work. And when lives depend on the answer, caution is always the right call.

I compare this process to heart surgery on a global stage. Teams get it right 99.99% of the time, but almost nobody notices. Their effort is monumental and continuous but largely anonymous. But when there is an outage, they are doing delicate, high-stakes work while the public watches the departure boards.

Get used to network outages

However, we’re about to hear a lot more about these teams because the rate of change in our infrastructure is rapidly accelerating. There are three reasons why:

  1. Decades-old systems are hitting their limits and must be modernized, as is the case with air traffic control. Modernization requires change, and change always involves risk.
  2. AI is putting new demands on networks. Agents and AI-powered applications are doing real work, and that work runs over infrastructure that can’t adequately carry it without growth and adaptation.
  3. AI brings a whole new set of security implications. This reason is the most urgent of the three. In my industry, we talk about the “patchpocalypse.” AI is helping uncover vulnerabilities faster than ever, some of which have been hidden for years or even decades. The time between discovery and exploitation has shrunk from a quarter or a year to mere hours. Every patch is a change to the network, and every change carries risk.

Put all of those factors together, and you get infrastructure that’s 30 or 40 years out of date and needs to change almost immediately. The networks themselves aren’t necessarily more fragile, but their criticality, complexity, and necessity for change are all growing faster than teams and funding can keep up. Everything is going to feel shaky for a while.

What IT leaders should do now

Many of the world’s most important networks are still managed largely by hand, with limited data, limited visibility, and limited tooling for governing change. That approach isn’t sustainable anymore. IT leaders need to make two critical investments:

  1. Give your teams real data about their infrastructure. They should know what the network is, how it’s interconnected, how it’s meant to be configured, and what’s happening on it right now. In a crisis, they should see at a glance the impact, the affected workloads, the change that likely caused it, and the downstream effects. When speed is essential, visibility is critical. Finding a problem is a major step toward solving it.
  2. Govern change before it reaches the network. Change drove all the high-profile outages in mid-November 2026. Teams need to understand the risk and behavior of a change before they make it. Modern patch windows are measured in hours rather than months. Teams need to build discipline into tools and processes.

The people running these networks are doing extraordinary work under extraordinary pressure with very little credit or recognition. The November outages demonstrate how much of the world’s economy and people’s daily lives depend on them. They deserve the data and the tools they need to keep networks running and avoid chaos.

#10554. Your SSL certificates can now last 200 days at most: The real risk isn’t renewal

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan. Following the latest update from the CA/Browser Forum, the maximum lifetime of a certificate has fallen from 398 days to 200, and it will drop to 100 days in March 2027 and 47 days in 2029. Renewal is no longer an annual chore. It’s an ongoing task that only stays manageable with automation.

So what does this mean if you already look after sites with SSL certificates, and will it bring drastic changes? For many setups, very little will change. For others, one missed renewal can mean an outage. This article explains what’s changing and what to do if you’re in the second group.

Today, an SSL certificate is valid for 200 days at most. The limit applies when a certificate is issued, so the ones you already hold keep their original expiration date.

Where you feel it depends on how your certificates renew. Sites on managed hosting platforms or behind a content delivery network (CDN) usually renew automatically already, often every 90 days, so the new limit changes little. The pressure lands on setups where someone buys a certificate once a year and installs it by hand. At 47 days, that becomes about 12 renewals a year.

A certificate is a promise from a certificate authority that a key really belongs to a domain, and that promise gets less reliable the longer it runs. If a private key leaks, or a certificate is issued by mistake, it stays usable until it expires. Cutting the lifetime shrinks that window, so a problem that once lingered for over a year is now fixed in weeks.

Shorter lifetimes also make revocation, the process for canceling a bad certificate, far less critical. Revocation has never worked perfectly, but a certificate that expires within weeks matters much less if a cancellation doesn’t reach every browser.

Another reason is about people. A task done once a year is easy to forget and hard to check from outside. Browser makers have pushed for years to move the industry onto automatic renewal, on the logic that a process that runs every few weeks gets tested constantly. If it breaks, you notice quickly instead of discovering it on the day the certificate expires.

For most people, the first effect is simply more work. A certificate that once needed attention every year will soon need it every few weeks. Plus, each renewal is a small chance for something to go wrong. Multiply that by dozens of sites, mail servers, and devices, and the chance of one slipping through grows quickly.

The safety nets are also thinner. If you relied on the renewal emails, nothing is watching your certificates now. Additionally, with a shorter life, there’s less time between this should have renewed and this has expired.

An expired certificate doesn’t make a site slow or dated. It makes it unreachable for most visitors. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all show a full-page warning that the connection isn’t private, and most people leave instead of clicking through. If the site uses HSTS, a setting that tells browsers to connect only over secure links, there is often no way to click through at all, and visitors are blocked outright until the certificate is fixed.

The damage doesn’t stop at the home page. Checkouts, contact forms, and logins that depend on the secure connection fail along with it, often without an error message that points at the real cause. Other systems break, too, because apps and integrations that call your site over a secure link refuse to connect to an expired certificate.

Nothing about your site has to change for any of this to happen. A date passes, and a site that worked on Friday is down on Monday. In a 47-day lifetime, that date comes around about every six weeks.

Automatic renewal tools do the heavy lifting well. The failures happen around them:

Look at the five failures above and you’ll see what they share. Each one happens quietly. The renewal job ran, or looked like it did, and nobody checked what the server was actually serving afterwards. Automation can tell you it tried. It can’t tell you the result reached your visitors.

What closes that gap is a check that never relies on your server’s own account of events. Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring does exactly that. It reads the certificate installed on your web server from the cloud, the way a visitor’s browser would, and alerts you before it expires, using thresholds you choose. If a renewal fails quietly, you hear about it from the monitor and not from a customer.

For each certificate, it records the issuing authority, the owner, the issue date, the expiration date, and the days remaining, including on servers that host several certificates behind one address. That last number matters more as lifespans shrink. When a certificate lasts 47 days, the days left is the figure that tells you a renewal is overdue, and you can set your warning against it using the quarter-of-the-lifetime rule covered next.

Once a monitor is watching your certificates, the next question is when it should speak up.

Most expiration alerts are set to a fixed number of days: warn at 30 days left and escalate at seven. That works for a certificate that lasts a year and renews with a month to spare. It breaks when the whole certificate lasts for a limited number of days.

Here’s why: a healthy certificate renews with about a third of its life still left. If your alert appears earlier than that, it goes off on certificates that are doing nothing wrong, and soon everyone ignores it. As lifespans shrink, a fixed 30-day alert will start doing exactly that.

The fix is to set the alerts based on lateness, not on how close the expiry date is. Warn when a quarter of the lifetime is left, since a renewal is overdue by then, and escalate when a tenth is left. Because these are shares of the lifetime, they keep working, however short lifespans get.

The next cut lands on March 15, 2027, so a few checks now will save you from scrambling later:

Shorter lifespans won’t break your site, but a missed renewal will, so fix the quiet failures now while a mistake still costs an afternoon to fix, not a Monday morning outage affecting lots of customers.

If you’d like a second pair of eyes on your certificates, you can start a 30-day free trial of Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring.

#10552. Review: Amazon’s Alexa Tablet 8 is a Fire Tablet with Google Play for $150 – what’s not to love?

Amazon shocked everyone in October when it launched its new Alexa Tablet series with Google Play support built-in, addressing the biggest shortcoming of its older Fire Tablets. For Black Friday 2026, the Alexa Tablet 8 is a mere $150 and, with Google Play on board, this feels like a Fire Tablet that’s all grown up.

The Alexa Tablet 8 is one of three new Amazon tablets that launched in October with Google Play on board, and it’s also the one I was personally the most excited about. I love a good tiny Android tablet, but there just aren’t that many out there – and some of the ones we do have are exorbitantly expensive.

Right up there with Amazon’s long-running reputation in the tablet space, Alexa Tablet 8 is very much an affordable device, and that’s reflected in its fairly meager specs:

Yet, I didn’t find myself put off by the device.

I specifically asked Amazon for a review unit of the absolute base model – 4GB of RAM and lockscreen ads – and I can say with confidence it’s Not Bad at the end of the day.

The display is objectively not good, but it’s not really trying to be flashy either. The panel gets bright enough for most indoor use and, for general browsing or watching videos around the house or even on a flight, it gets the job done. If anything, my biggest complaint on the display was just how smudgey it gets with fingerprints.

Hardware is a strong suit. The Alexa Tablet 8 has an aluminum build that comes in this gorgeous teal color as well as a softer “Rosette” pink (or “Graphite,” if you want to keep it boring). It’s thin and light and slips into a bag easily, and even fit into the back pocket of my jeans. Buttons are clicky and aspects such as the speakers actually do well enough – like the display, the speakers aren’t good, but they’re not bad by any stretch either.

Amazon has a folio cover available that’s simple but nice, with a fabric finish that’s grippy. It’s an extra $40, though, which feels like a bit much for a super-affordable Android slate.

The biggest question was around the software experience, and this is where this new effort really shines.

Alexa Tablet 8 ships with Android 16 out of the box, not FireOS or whatever Amazon was calling its forked experience on Fire Tablets (I genuinely refuse to go double-check because it’s a memory I’m thrilled to never have to revisit). It’s a pretty “stock” experience, with Amazon leaving aspects such as the notification shade/quick settings alone, and even the Settings menu feels pretty clean.

That’s not to say nothing has changed. The homescreen has a fairly standard layout , but with these neat little corner widgets – one a “dynamic” widget with scrolling content (mostly ads) and the other a shortcut for Alexa search. Amazon is pushing Alexa as a voice assistant pretty heavily on these tablets, but I’m happy to report it’s pretty easy to ignore if you choose. These tablets will be great additions to your Alexa ecosystem if you’re invested, but I’m simply not.

The biggest change you’ll find is the lockscreen, where Amazon’s base models all come with lockscreen ads. This saves you about $20 on the hardware, and it’s not that bad of an experience. That said, I’d absolutely spend the extra $20 at purchase to go without them, especially seeing as this blocks the ability to set a lockscreen wallpaper at all. It doesn’t cost anything more to remove them later, though, with a $20 charge through your Amazon account removing ads.

But what’s important here is that, for the fire time, Amazon is admitting defeat and installing the Google Play Store.

Alexa Tablet 8, and the rest of the lineup, has Google Play out of the box and access to any app you want. This means that you can, if you choose, fully ignore Amazon’s own services and do whatever you want. The smallest of examples: While Amazon’s built-in keyboard is fine, it’s wonderful that I don’t have to jump through hoops to switch over to Gboard. Fire Tablets were always an enticing value with a big catch, but Amazon’s change in this regard truly makes Alexa Tablets an attractive option for everyone – not just those willing to put up with the restriction or put in the work to hack Google apps on board.

Performance, despite the meager specs, is not awful. MediaTek’s low-end chip has just enough horsepower for general use, and 4GB of RAM isn’t as detrimental as I would have expected. It’s not fast by any means, but you could do a lot worse. There are 4GB Android tablets I’ve literally decided not to review because I couldn’t use them past the setup process, so the fact that Amazon is delivering a completely usable experience is a win in my book, even more so that I don’t actually mind using it. There’s a caveat to that, of course, and it’s that you shouldn’t expect to do a ton on this base model. For light browsing, reading Kindle books (or whatever other reading app since, you know, Google Play), or watching videos, this is great. For games, you’ll want to look elsewhere (and expect to spend more).

Alexa Tablet 8 isn’t some shining example of a perfect budget tablet, but I think it really nails the fundamentals. At its usual $230~ starting price, it’s a plenty-good deal for those in the market for an affordable Android slate, but the Black Friday pricing of just $150 is all the better – I just wish the model with 8GB of RAM was also on sale.

Amazon’s pivot to Alexa Tablets is great – though I hope the company knows full well that everyone is still going to call these Fire Tablets or Kindles or whatever combination of brands that spring to mind. But that reputation might work in Amazon’s favor at the end of the day. While there’s a huge portion of the audience that’s been left frustrated for years at the lack of Play Store support on Fire Tablets, they’ve still been a market success for the most part, so this shift is just a win for everyone. Users get a better experience, Amazon gets to shuffle its priorities away from a dead app store, and the market as a whole gets an affordable piece of hardware that doesn’t suck.

#10551. This holiday season, the best meal deals come with a side of merch

Socks aren’t usually something kids want for Christmas. McDonald’s is betting adults will want them with their meal, though.

Instead of a plastic toy, the chain is offering free pairs of ugly Christmas socks with every purchase of its Home Alone-themed specialty meal, which will arrive in stores December 1. With each order, customers will get one of four pairs of festive socks featuring illustrations of McDonald’s characters like Grimace, or Macaulay Culkin’s Home Alone character, Kevin McCallister.

McDonald’s isn’t alone in this. The socks, designed in the style of an ugly Christmas sweater, are kitschy collectibles that fit within the broader trend of apparel releases by food and quick service brands, and it’s bigger than ever this holiday season. Burger King and Wendy’s are also giving away cold weather gear —both happen to be beanies, and Burger King’s is Peanuts-themed—with their holiday meal deals this year, too.

Restaurants and food brands have turned to clothing and apparel in recent years to capitalize on “post-ironic” cultural relevance and to deepen brand affinity even as shoppers pull back on spending. Chains like Cava have released their own ingredient-themed apparel collections, while other brands have turned to unconventional partnerships, like PringlesCrocs or Hidden Valley Ranch-flavored chapstick. For some fans, restaurant merch has become the new band T-shirt.

The happy-meal-toys-for-adults trend also comes as grown-ups are increasingly ordering kids meals, according to the market research firm Circana, which found adult orders of kids meals are up 28% since 2019. At Burger King, the No. 2 U.S. burger chain by sales behind McDonald’s, sales of its King Jr. meal are up 40% year over year, which the chain attributes in part to more adult purchases with no kids around.

Designing a kids meal for adults, then, is catering to an already growing customer base. Instead of giving them toys with their meals, apparel is a giveaway that’s usable.

Due to rising prices, customers have dined out less frequently over the past two years; to win them back, chains are focusing on quality and value. Though McDonald’s has fared better than many of its competitors, it announced a 0.2% decline in U.S. sales on its earnings call this month. To grow its domestic business, the chain is rolling out new menu items with smaller portion sizes and more protein, as well as leaning into specialty drinks and dirty sodas. Meals themed around nostalgic IP like Home Alone add up to another tactic.

McDonald’s is marketing the meal as an invitation to “leave adulthood behind” by tapping into nostalgia, and letting the customers customize their meals by picking their own entrée. It also leans into Home Alone through its menu items: french fries rebranded as “Little Nero’s Pizza McShaker Fries” for the film’s fictional pizza chain, along with a McFlurry, and pizza-flavored seasoning packet and dipping sauce.

This is what a kids meal looks like when it’s “kidulting.”

#10548. Starbucks’ viral Bearista cup is back for the holidays. Here’s how they turned the cute cup into a collector frenzy

Starbucks obviously knows coffee, but the chain has also mastered the ability to sell endlessly collectible merchandise. Collecting its mugs and cold cups has been a hobby of die-hard fans and online content creators who make videos about hunting for the latest drop, and interest in Starbucks merchandise reaches a fever pitch around the holidays.

In November 2025, the company introduced the Starbucks Bearista Glass Cold Cup in the U.S. The handblown, bear-shaped glass cup for cold drinks came with a Starbucks-green beanie and a green-and-white striped straw that proved irresistible. Lines snaked around stores before their early-morning openings. More than one store witnessed physical fights, and videos on social media of people “hunting” the cup racked up views.

The Bearista has been a recurring mascot for the brand since 1997, when Starbucks introduced a plush, green-aproned bear for the holidays. In 2023, it morphed into a cold cup in Korea, then spread throughout Asia before hitting the U.S. last November. By then it was already on cup collectors’ radars.

Dana Pellicano, SVP of global product experience, Starbucks: We were seeing this trend of kidulting, adults leaning into playful, fun products. The confluence of that, [the bear’s legacy], and the rise of cold drinks made it the right time for us to bring it to the U.S.

Carol Casey, aka RayahSunshine, cup collector/content creator: In the cup community, we see lots of cups coming out of other countries that are really enticing. We noticed that Starbucks Asia had a very unique set of cups. Their cups were more cutesy.

The artisan quality of the cup meant its supply was very limited. That created demand for social media videos of how to find one, and even created a secondary market on eBay. In a statement, the company apologized to those who weren’t able to snag one.

Pellicano: What makes it special is also what makes it logistically hard and part of the reason we had to be really disciplined about how we launched it. When you say yes to something, you’re saying no to something else. So we are saying yes to this really premium, elevated offering and therefore unintentionally saying no to everybody being able to have one. These are the choices that you have to balance.

Lindsay Ream, Starbucks coffeehouse leader, Grand Rapids, Michigan: Everybody wanted it. We get to the store at 4 a.m.—we open at 4:30—and when we got here, we had six cars in the parking lot waiting for us to open the doors. All day long the phone rang. We had someone answering all day to say “sorry, we’re sold out.”

Casey: Because stores stagger their openings and resellers pop from store to store, it’s very competitive. I like to go where I know I can for sure get the cup. With the limited editions, you’re there at 3 a.m., and some people were getting there at 2. The Bearista bear went nuts. Everybody was trying to get it—and people were willing to spend $250 on eBay for it. It was so limited that it upset people more than not, but it did bring a lot of interest.

Since last year, Starbucks has launched four more Bearista cups—the Pink Drink Bearista with a white hat and strawberry straw topper, an online-exclusive, soccer-themed Bearista for Starbucks Rewards Reserve tier members, and a Snoopy-shaped cup for fall. For the holiday season, the original Bearista is making a comeback, with a surprise box that contains one of four variations on the original, with the potential to include a rare golden Bearista..

Pellicano: We’ve really worked to refine our processes, and we’ve had a lot of success. We try to match the natural demand of where our stores see real volume in driving merch. We capped how many cups customers can purchase [at two per person].

Ream: In my district, we talked about partners not buying cups ahead of time. We have “partner access” where employees only were offered an early launch, but it didn’t come out of the amount of cups that we had for customers.

Casey: I may hunt it [again] just for the sake of the hunt and the content—just because that’s what I do.

Simply inserting a cartridge into the speaker gives you access to all soundtracks and sound effects, which can be controlled using onboard physical controls including next, previous, and volume.

#10545. I voiced a character in ‘Grand Theft Auto.’ I never expected her to follow me for 17 years

The release of Grand Theft Auto VI generated more than $1.65 billion in preorder sales, broke internet usage records, and shattered streaming records on platforms like Twitch and YouTube. For millennials who played video games growing up, this is a cultural moment.

For me, as someone who works in digital editorial and audience engagement for a media company that covers tech and news, the data is staggering. It also reminds me of when I stumbled into the Grand Theft Auto universe in my twenties.

In 2009, I was fresh out of Tisch School of the Arts at New York University and was auditioning endlessly. I spent my days at castings surrounded by dozens of other girls who looked like me, only prettier. I spent my nights waitressing until the wee hours of the morning, or haphazardly attending parties and clubs where I admittedly hoped to be discovered. These were chaotic times: years of small successes, like a role on Law & Order or a bit part on a soap opera, separated by months upon months of fruitless auditions and absolutely no work.

So when a friend from high school reached out to me about a gig recording voice-over for The Ballad of Gay Tony, a 2009 expansion of Grand Theft Auto IV, I quickly accepted without asking many questions or seeing the script. To be frank, I wouldn’t have known what to ask about how the character interacted with the universe of GTA. My parents were strict, especially about video games. They were both educators and categorized video games as brain rot before that was even a thing, so I’d never played GTA before.

I recorded Joni’s voice track in a couple of hours at Rockstar Games in SoHo, with my high school friend in the audio booth. This was the easiest acting job—there hadn’t been any awkward audition, all of my scenes were set in a nightclub, which was an environment I knew well, and I didn’t have to memorize anything. I just had a sheet of one-liners to deliver in a sassy club manager voice. Since I was a waitress at the time, I remember using one of my managers from The Coffee Shop on Union Square as inspiration. (I won’t name her out of respect.)

I needed to separate the character from myself because I wasn’t half as bold as Joni, who spent a lot of time propositioning Luis while simultaneously mocking his, er, body part size. It seems important to note that I didn’t realize players could interact with characters beyond speaking to them—in ways that are both violent and sexually violent—but I’m not sure I would’ve turned down the job even if I had known. After all, Joni was a character, she was just an avatar, and I was an actress. I left the studio with few regrets, and even fewer when the check cleared on time.

This was 2009. The term “digital footprint” wasn’t part of the zeitgeist. Instagram didn’t exist, and I still typed websites I liked into my browser to check the news—and none of those sites covered gamer culture. Could I have anticipated that Grand Theft Auto would remain a cultural phenomenon that would follow me forever? I don’t think so.

I also didn’t run in circles where “fandoms” were a thing, so I was surprised when fans of Joni started emailing me in 2010. In hindsight, this speaks to the growing popularity of the GTA franchise, and the fact that Joni was probably a lot of people’s cup of tea. Their emails were typically short and bizarre, and a few were desperate for a response. It takes a lot of deep thinking about a character to research the voice-over actor and email her, but if there’s one skill I already possessed at age 26, it was knowing that often no response is the best response.

Not long after I recorded my voice-over for GTA, I began to suspect I had skills beyond acting. Motivated by the fact that I never felt particularly intrigued by the scripts I was given to audition for, I created my own web series, took a job managing social media and, through a combination of hard work and luck, very quickly built a media career. In 2011 or 2012, I took my acting website down and the emails stopped. When Instagram introduced direct messages, the messages returned, but at a slower pace.

During the pandemic, I managed an editorial team that included a section dedicated to gaming. I’d all but forgotten about Joni, but decided to trot out my voice-over credit as a fun fact during one of those team meetings where we were all trying to bond as humans while working from home in isolation. When we finally returned to the office, one of the producers who’d been on the call brought me a poster of Joni as a gift.

I unrolled it at my desk. There she was, a reminder of a period in my life when any job that was even moderately creative seemed preferable to serving mojitos. On the poster, Joni is happy as can be, spraying champagne into the air and grinning in her pink dress. It dawned on me that some of the people on my team had been teenagers when the game came out. I thanked the producer and tried not to imagine what sorts of interactions he might have had with Joni.

I’ve managed to scrub much of my twenties from the internet—a feat I suspect only elder millennials will be able to pull off, as the internet grows more permanent and everyone becomes increasingly obsessed with saving “receipts.” But Joni is still out there. She occasionally resurfaces in my professional life, partly because Rockstar Games remains a cultural force, and partly because the way players interact with characters—especially women—is still a conversation worth having.

I’ve spent years putting distance between myself and the person I was when I voiced her. Joni, meanwhile, is still in that pink dress, spraying champagne, having the time of her life.

#10543. Affordable AI takes more than a lower price

Elizabeth Field DiGiovanni runs Parcel Air, which makes travel activity boxes designed to keep young children occupied on flights. Everything that goes into the Los Angeles solopreneur’s boxes has to come from somewhere: the toys, the crayons, the packaging. Most of the factories she works with are in Asia, where the workday begins around the time Elizabeth is putting her 4-year-old and her 2-year-old to bed.

She was sourcing—finding factories that could make what she needed and getting the job quoted. Those questions run in sequence; each answer sets up the next. A minimum order quantity changes which price break to ask about. A certification answer decides whether lead time matters at all. With the time difference, every link in that chain cost her a day. One vendor negotiation took more than three weeks to produce a quote.

AI agents for e-commerce could have done that work for her. Elizabeth assumed reaching that point meant a week of setup she could not spare, choosing among tools and connecting her catalog and supplier list. Now one of our customers, Elizabeth told us when discussing a case study that while running a company she was also minding two small children at home, and there is rarely a free minute.

AI AFFORDABILITY

Affordability, for a business like hers, includes the total cost of adoption.

A Goldman Sachs survey conducted in August found that 86% of surveyed alumni of its 10,000 Small Businesses program were using AI, but only 15% had fully integrated it into their core operations. Those owners completed a business education program, so they generally sit ahead of small firms. Separately, Census Bureau data from December 2025 to May 2026 showed AI use below 20% among U.S. employer businesses with four or fewer employees, compared with 37% among those with at least 250.

Meanwhile, Stanford’s 2025 AI Index tracked the cost of querying a model at roughly GPT-3.5-level performance from $20 per million tokens in November 2022 to $0.07 by October 2024. We have watched the same curve inside our own product, Accio, where token cost fell by half in four months while consumption grew tenfold. Lowering the cost of intelligence still leaves the work required to put it to use.

THE COSTS BEYOND THE SUBSCRIPTION

Someone still has to configure the tools, understand the business questions, and check the results. Larger companies can spread that work across teams. Parcel Air has no employees, so Elizabeth performs all of it. Those demands belong in any affordability calculation. The companies building these systems, ours included, can lower them at three levels.

1. Lower the technical barrier

An owner looking for suppliers should be able to start with that job, without first learning model selection, prompt engineering, or software integration. Without dedicated IT teams, small businesses have little capacity to assemble and maintain AI systems.

Pre-configured expert agents and sourcing plugins do that work in advance, reducing the configuration, custom development, and integration an owner would otherwise take on.

2. Close the expertise gap

For AI agents for e-commerce to deliver value, they must combine technical simplicity with an understanding of how businesses source, trade, and operate.

A tariff changes landed cost. A missing certification can prevent goods from entering a market. Supplier screening and international logistics require knowledge that owners without procurement teams may not have.

Developers can embed that knowledge inside the owner’s workflow. Owners should still be able to see what needs checking, with the system flagging missing information and claims requiring documentation.

3. Make autonomy easier to trust

An agent that requires constant supervision can create as much work as it removes. Unlimited authority, however, introduces risks an owner may not be able to afford.

Owners need clear permissions, a visible record of actions, and the ability to inspect recommendations and intervene. Routine supplier research and organizing quotes can run independently once the workflow is proven. Orders, payments, and contractual commitments should require explicit human approval.

Those controls belong in the product itself. The goal is less routine supervision while the owner keeps control over consequential decisions.

WHAT CHANGED FOR PARCEL AIR

Elizabeth sources through Alibaba.com and runs this work on Accio, our AI agent designed for small businesses and solo founders. She briefs it the way she would brief a colleague. Before bed, she writes out what she needs: the product, her target cost, the safety certifications, and the quantity. The agents work with suppliers through the business day in Asia while she sleeps. In the morning, before the children are up, she reads what came back and makes the call. She described it to us as having an entire APAC team on the night shift.

The first time she ran it properly, she says, the AI went through 68 suppliers in 3 minutes and 17 seconds. A quote that used to take three weeks came back in 12 hours.

She still sets the target cost. She still decides which supplier to trust and which certification claim needs a document behind it. What changed was the waiting. She stopped losing a day to every question, and she got her evenings back.

MEASURE THE FULL COST OF ADOPTION

Those of us who build AI tools for small businesses should be able to answer two questions. How much time does it take an owner to get a useful result, including setup and learning? And how much time does the tool save on recurring tasks once you factor in setup, review, and upkeep?

For a small business owner, the real test comes when the tool becomes part of a busy workweek. Small businesses everywhere should be able to afford to put AI to work. As Elizabeth puts it, “You don’t need a bigger team. You need the night shift covered.”

Kuo Zhang is president of Global B2B Business at Alibaba Ecommerce Group.

#10541. Cities built 311—teachers need one, too

As a 27-year veteran physics teacher, 2011 Connecticut State Teacher of the Year, and 2023 inductee into the national teachers’ hall of fame, Kristen Record knew how to teach. But last year, she ran up against the limits of her vast knowledge base when she stepped in to fill a vacancy and teach honors chemistry at her suburban high school in Stratford, CT.

In a phone interview with this article’s coauthor, Talia Milgrom-Elcott, Record described a student who loved science but whose severe dyslexia made chemistry, with its letters, numbers, and subscripts, a challenge. Working with his parents and a special education coordinator, Record turned to the internet, YouTube, and AI for answers. She lacked the knowledge and tools to support him on her own, and because none of the other science or special education teachers had any expertise in this area, she had nowhere else to turn.

As more AI tools and edtech platforms enter the scene, the marketplace of information teachers turn to for support has become more crowded and confusing, even for those working inside their areas of expertise. The abundance of available tools places the burden on teachers to determine which are effective, for which students, and under what circumstances, often with little guidance or support.

LESSONS FROM LOCAL GOVERNMENT AND MEDICINE

New York City had a version of this problem. Residents faced more than 40 agency call centers and no clear way to know which to call. In 2003, the city launched 311, a single number for every non-emergency question, reachable by phone, text, app, or web. By 2022, it had received at least 500 million contacts, and cities around the world have copied it.

Medicine has UpToDate, a clinical reference written and continually updated by more than 7,000 paid physician authors and reviewers. A doctor unsure of how to treat something gets a practical synthesis of the current evidence instead of a stack of raw studies.

Both examples point to something education still lacks: a “Teacher 311.” This single go-to source would turn scattered expertise into clear answers that teachers can depend on. Building one would take rethinking and reinvesting in our nation’s education research infrastructure.

HOW A TEACHER 311 COULD WORK

A Teacher 311 could look like a texting-based hotline crossed with a living research engine. A teacher like Record could text or chat a question: How do I teach symbolic chemistry notation to a student with severe dyslexia? They would get back a specific, vetted answer instead of an unwieldy list of search results.

Behind the scenes, master teachers, researchers, and school system leaders—paid for their expertise—would brainstorm suggestions and review AI-generated recommendations. They would set the standards for what the system would draw on: peer-reviewed research and educator-verified practices. Privacy protections would be built in from the start.

As quality is proven and trust earned, AI could take on more of the first draft, but an expert would still review every answer. Teachers would rate responses, so the system improves with each question. The best answers to common questions would proactively go out to teacher networks and professional associations nationwide. Questions without ready answers would fuel the pipeline for education R&D; those asked most often or with the highest potential impact on students would be prioritized.

For years, the Institute of Education Sciences and U.S. Department of Education have been urging researchers to focus on “knowledge mobilization”: closing the gap between what research tells us and what reaches teachers and students. A Teacher 311 could be that bridge.

WHAT’S NEEDED TO CREATE TEACHER 311

The idea for Teacher 311 came from Talia, who developed the concept and the plan to build it. Partnering with Alliance for Learning Innovation (ALI) made sense given its work on federal education R&D policy. ALI’s latest policy brief asks the federal government to build that infrastructure—the capacity to research and test ideas like Teacher 311 before they scale, so the ones that reach classrooms actually work.

Senators Bennet (D-CO), Tillis (R-NC), and Van Hollen (D-MD) echoed that call in September when they reintroduced the New Essential Education Discoveries (NEED) Act. If passed, the bill would create the kind of agile center that could seed the investment to build and scale a project like Teacher 311. The federal government is well positioned to back something like this, and an administration that did could make it a signature service and a hallmark of its tenure.

In the meantime, the private and philanthropic sectors have the opportunity to move the needle now. We estimate that the Teacher 311 hub would cost less than $5 million to build and $3 million per year to run, a fraction of the $2.55 billion the federal government allocated in fiscal year 2022 for education R&D (the year ALI conducted a funding analysis). Done right, the payoff would reach every level of the system. The Institute of Education Sciences and the National Science Foundation would gain a steady, practitioner-driven pipeline of research questions worth funding. States and districts would get better evidence on where to invest in professional learning. Most importantly, teachers would get useful, trusted guidance on the problems they’re facing, and their students would benefit.

Teachers search for solutions every day to help their students. Record figured it out eventually, mostly on her own. The next teacher with a student like hers shouldn’t have to.

Sara Schapiro is executive director of Alliance for Learning Innovation. Talia Milgrom-Elcott is cofounder and executive director of Beyond100K and Starfish Institute.
